ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Half (n=459) of the participants were randomised to practise a common psychotherapeutic technique-cognitive distancing-throughout the task.

> Research across economics, psychology, and health sciences suggests the answer to this question-your subjective well-being-is closely tied to objective quality of life 1, 2 and health across the lifespan 3 .

> Half (49.1%) of the participants were randomised to an acute psychological intervention known as "cognitive distancing", a common 42 and effective 43 core component of psychological therapy which alters choice behaviour in this task 41 and may hence modulate affective dynamics.

> All participants saw the same six symbols, but the pairs were randomised across individuals and counterbalanced across trials.

> Participants were also asked at the end of each of the sixty-trial training blocks to rate (from 0-100) how fatigued they felt compared to the beginning of the block.

> After six training blocks, participants were tested on all fifteen unique pairs without feedback.

> Half of the participants (n=459; 49.1%) were randomised to be taught, and then practise throughout the task, a psychotherapeutic technique termed "cognitive distancing", which encouraged them to "take a step back" from their emotional reactions to feedback throughout the task (see Dercon et al. [41] for further details).

> Drift over time in affect may be particularly relevant to our task, as participants were able to take as long as they wished to rate their subjective feelings, and time between blocks was additionally unconstrained.

> Specifically, there was strong evidence for a negative distancing by fatigue interaction for both measures of fatigue, such that while there was no association between β and post-block fatigue (mean or change over time) in non-distanced participants, distanced participants had lower inverse temperatures (i.e., choices less determined by expected values) with increases in self-reported fatigue (e.g., mean [95% HDI] difference in change in β for a 10-point increase in mean post-block fatigue in distanced versus non-distanced participants = -0.129 [-0.278, -0.028], P direction = 0.990; Figure S6Aiii).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.377", "p = 0.938", "p=0.376"), Sentence = c("We found no statistical evidence that either differed between groups (enjoyment: t(933) = -0.88, p = 0.377; concentration: t(933) = 0.08, p = 0.938), suggesting that the addition of the distancing instruction did not render the task appreciably more effortful or less enjoyable overall.", "We found no statistical evidence that either differed between groups (enjoyment: t(933) = -0.88, p = 0.377; concentration: t(933) = 0.08, p = 0.938), suggesting that the addition of the distancing instruction did not render the task appreciably more effortful or less enjoyable overall.", "To explore similarities between the effects of this psychological intervention and those of a pharmacological treatment-antidepressant medication-we also asked participants to report their current medication use: 130 participants (69 distanced [15.0%] and 61 non-distanced [12.8%]; no statistical evidence of a difference: χ 2 (1)=0.78, p=0.376) reported current antidepressant use, with the majority (n=92; 70.8%) taking an SSRI (Table S3)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Half (n=459) of the participants were randomised to practise a common psychotherapeutic technique-cognitive distancing-throughout the task.

Research across economics, psychology, and health sciences suggests the answer to this question-your subjective well-being-is closely tied to objective quality of life 1, 2 and health across the lifespan 3 .

Half (49.1%) of the participants were randomised to an acute psychological intervention known as "cognitive distancing", a common 42 and effective 43 core component of psychological therapy which alters choice behaviour in this task 41 and may hence modulate affective dynamics.
All participants saw the same six symbols, but the pairs were randomised across individuals and counterbalanced across trials.
Participants were also asked at the end of each of the sixty-trial training blocks to rate (from 0-100) how fatigued they felt compared to the beginning of the block.
After six training blocks, participants were tested on all fifteen unique pairs without feedback.

Half of the participants (n=459; 49.1%) were randomised to be taught, and then practise throughout the task, a psychotherapeutic technique termed "cognitive distancing", which encouraged them to "take a step back" from their emotional reactions to feedback throughout the task (see Dercon et al. [41] for further details).

Drift over time in affect may be particularly relevant to our task, as participants were able to take as long as they wished to rate their subjective feelings, and time between blocks was additionally unconstrained.

Specifically, there was strong evidence for a negative distancing by fatigue interaction for both measures of fatigue, such that while there was no association between β and post-block fatigue (mean or change over time) in non-distanced participants, distanced participants had lower inverse temperatures (i.e., choices less determined by expected values) with increases in self-reported fatigue (e.g., mean [95% HDI] difference in change in β for a 10-point increase in mean post-block fatigue in distanced versus non-distanced participants = -0.129 [-0.278, -0.028], P direction = 0.990; Figure S6Aiii).

text.text: Affective states are dynamic, fluctuating in response to recent events: an unexpected pleasure, a disappointing loss.
Affective biases, which cause disruptions in these dynamics, are core components of mental ill-health, but the specific effects of treatments on these biases are poorly understood.

Here, we investigate the impact of common psychiatric treatments on subjective assessments of happiness, confidence, and engagement during a reinforcement learning task (N =935; 130 taking antidepressant medications).
Half (n=459) of the participants were randomised to practise a common psychotherapeutic technique-cognitive distancing-throughout the task.
From a joint computational model of learning and affect, we find evidence for distinct and overlapping impacts of psychiatric treatments on affective dynamics.
Cognitive distancing attenuates downward drift in happiness and increases recency bias in the affective impact of recent choices.

Conversely, antidepressant use increases baseline happiness and confidence in individuals with similar levels of current symptoms, and decreases recency bias such that more past events influence affective states.

Crucially, both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use converge to dampen negative biases in happiness and confidence specifically in participants experiencing higher levels of anxiety and depression symptoms.
Together, our results indicate that common treatments for mental ill-health may alter symptoms through their impact on affective dynamics, but via distinct mechanisms.
How are you feeling right now?

Research across economics, psychology, and health sciences suggests the answer to this question-your subjective well-being-is closely tied to objective quality of life 1, 2 and health across the lifespan 3 .
text.formatted: Research across economics, psychology, and health sciences suggests the answer to this question-your subjective well-being-is closely tied to objective quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> and health across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: But feelings are far from static, momentarily fluctuating in response to recent events [4] [5] [6] , and even individual choices.
text.formatted: But feelings are far from static, momentarily fluctuating in response to recent events <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> , and even individual choices.

text.text: Frequently asking participants to rate their feelings enables a read-out of moment-to-moment changes in subjective well-being, or their affective dynamics.
Affective dynamics are closely coupled with objective quantities that drive choices during learning.

In influential work, Rutledge et al. [5] demonstrated that momentary happiness ratings during a gambling task could be accurately predicted by a computational model incorporating the average reward for a gamble (expected value) and the outcome of the gamble minus this average (prediction error).

Using a task where reward magnitude and probability were uncorrelated, Blain & Rutledge [7] subsequently showed that momentary happiness is particularly sensitive to changes in learningrelated quantities-specifically, prediction errors for reward probability-as compared to reward information that was relevant to behaviour but not learning.
text.formatted: Using a task where reward magnitude and probability were uncorrelated, Blain & Rutledge [7] subsequently showed that momentary happiness is particularly sensitive to changes in learningrelated quantities-specifically, prediction errors for reward probability-as compared to reward information that was relevant to behaviour but not learning.

text.text: Links between momentary happiness ratings and learning-related quantities may extend to subjective assessments of other affective states.

Theoretical accounts posit that momentary confidence is the approximate probability a choice is correct [8] [9] [10] , though empirical studies have shown that confidence judgements also reflect uncertainty in the task-relevant estimate, with individuals differing in how strongly they weight the two 11 , and that, where several options compete, momentary confidence appears better explained by simpler comparisons between the available choices 12 .

text.text: Effort costs, meanwhile, influence momentary engagement by decreasing the value of choices independently of reward probability 13, 14 , and the fatigue and boredom that build with exertion have been proposed to signal when to disengage from a task 15 .
text.formatted: Effort costs, meanwhile, influence momentary engagement by decreasing the value of choices independently of reward probability <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , and the fatigue and boredom that build with exertion have been proposed to signal when to disengage from a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, the links between affective dynamics and choice behaviour are cyclic 16 : induced changes (biases) in affect alter choice behaviour by modulating expected values 17 , perhaps to favour more informative outcomes 18 .
text.formatted: Furthermore, the links between affective dynamics and choice behaviour are cyclic <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> : induced changes (biases) in affect alter choice behaviour by modulating expected values <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , perhaps to favour more informative outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Affective dynamics may therefore be recoverable from the trial-wise structure of choices and outcomes during learning.
Biases in affective dynamics are a core feature of mental ill-health and may be a target of psychiatric treatments [19] [20] [21] .
text.formatted: Biases in affective dynamics are a core feature of mental ill-health and may be a target of psychiatric treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> .

text.text: Symptoms of depression have been consistently linked to lower 7, 22 and less stable 23, 24 momentary happiness, while transdiagnostic features of mental ill-health have been linked to biased confidence judgements at different timescales [25] [26] [27] [28] and impairments in motivation and engagement 14, [29] [30] [31] .

text.text: Theoretical accounts building on classic cognitive models 32 posit that affective biases precipitate symptoms of mental ill-health by inducing changes in "bottom-up" emotion processing and perception 33 ; over time, by shifting "top-down" cognitive processes such as attention and memory, affective biases may maintain symptoms and become self-reinforcing 20 .
text.formatted: Theoretical accounts building on classic cognitive models <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> posit that affective biases precipitate symptoms of mental ill-health by inducing changes in "bottom-up" emotion processing and perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> ; over time, by shifting "top-down" cognitive processes such as attention and memory, affective biases may maintain symptoms and become self-reinforcing <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Computationally, the biased perception of environmental outcomes can be interpreted as modulating the (learned) value of associated choices 34 , which may explain the altered choice behaviour frequently observed in patients with depression and anxiety 35, 36.
text.formatted: Computationally, the biased perception of environmental outcomes can be interpreted as modulating the (learned) value of associated choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> , which may explain the altered choice behaviour frequently observed in patients with depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref>.

text.text: Dampening of affective biases has thus been proposed as a candidate mechanism for the therapeutic effects of psychiatric treatments 20 .
text.formatted: Dampening of affective biases has thus been proposed as a candidate mechanism for the therapeutic effects of psychiatric treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, acute selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) administration reverses negative perceptual biases in depressed participants 37 , while an acute cognitive psychotherapeutic intervention was recently shown to specifically target negative biases in self-attribution of the outcomes of everyday events 38 .
text.formatted: Indeed, acute selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) administration reverses negative perceptual biases in depressed participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> , while an acute cognitive psychotherapeutic intervention was recently shown to specifically target negative biases in self-attribution of the outcomes of everyday events <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: However, the precise links between (biases in) choices, affect, and psychiatric symptoms-and whether affective dynamics may be a transdiagnostic treatment target of psychological and pharmacological interventions for symptoms of mental illhealth-remain unclear.

Here, we asked online participants (N =935) to rate their feelings on one of three different affect scales-happiness, confidence, and engagement-after receiving feedback on each choice they made in a reinforcement learning (RL) task [39] [40] [41] (Figure 1A).

text.text: Half (49.1%) of the participants were randomised to an acute psychological intervention known as "cognitive distancing", a common 42 and effective 43 core component of psychological therapy which alters choice behaviour in this task 41 and may hence modulate affective dynamics.

text.text: As antidepressants target neuromodulatory systems involved in choice behaviour 44 , we also collected information on current antidepressant medication use in a demographic questionnaire (reported by 13.9% of participants), and derived transdiagnostic mental health symptom factor scores from a psychiatric questionnaire battery 45, 46 .

text.text: We then formalised affect ratings as a function of learning-related quantities derived from participants' choices in a computational model, allowing us to map individuals' affective dynamics onto the same trialwise signals that shape behaviour.

The reinforcement learning task in the present study-the probabilistic selection task 39, 40 -involved learning which symbol in each of three pairs was more likely correct (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: The reinforcement learning task in the present study-the probabilistic selection task <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> -involved learning which symbol in each of three pairs was more likely correct (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>).

text.text: Correct answers were rewarded with 25 points, and so consistent choice of the "better" symbol in each pair enabled a participant to accumulate more "Correct" feedback and more points (and maximise their chances of winning a monetary bonus, which was contingent on their performance relative to other participants).

One symbol in each pair was always more likely correct, but the contingencies varied across the pairs, from 0.8/0.2 ('AB') to 0.7/0.3 ('CD'), to 0.6/0.4 ('EF'), meaning that, for the pairs with closer contingencies, consistently choosing the most-likely correct symbol would be accompanied by more frequent paradoxical feedback.
All participants saw the same six symbols, but the pairs were randomised across individuals and counterbalanced across trials.
After making a choice, participants received verbal feedback ("Correct!"
or "Incorrect")-if "Correct!", they were always also shown their current point total increasing by 25 points-and then rated their subjective happiness, confidence, or engagement.
One of the three questions was asked after each trial outcome, with each question asked twenty times per block of sixty trials, and never more than twice in a row.
Participants were also asked at the end of each of the sixty-trial training blocks to rate (from 0-100) how fatigued they felt compared to the beginning of the block.
After six training blocks, participants were tested on all fifteen unique pairs without feedback.
We previously reported the effects of cognitive distancing on task performance and learning, including results of the test phase, in the same sample 41.
text.formatted: We previously reported the effects of cognitive distancing on task performance and learning, including results of the test phase, in the same sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref>.

text.text: Half of the participants (n=459; 49.1%) were randomised to be taught, and then practise throughout the task, a psychotherapeutic technique termed "cognitive distancing", which encouraged them to "take a step back" from their emotional reactions to feedback throughout the task (see Dercon et al. [41] for further details).

Apart from an additional instructional video before the task started and a small prompt to "Distance yourself..." which appeared with each fixation cross (Figure 1A), the task was identical for distanced and non-distanced participants.
text.formatted: Apart from an additional instructional video before the task started and a small prompt to "Distance yourself..." which appeared with each fixation cross (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>), the task was identical for distanced and non-distanced participants.

text.text: On completing the study, participants rated how much they had enjoyed the task and how well they had concentrated during it.

We found no statistical evidence that either differed between groups (enjoyment: t(933) = -0.88, p = 0.377; concentration: t(933) = 0.08, p = 0.938), suggesting that the addition of the distancing instruction did not render the task appreciably more effortful or less enjoyable overall.
We did not, however, ask participants directly about their use of the technique, and so lack a measure of adherence to the intervention itself.

To explore similarities between the effects of this psychological intervention and those of a pharmacological treatment-antidepressant medication-we also asked participants to report their current medication use: 130 participants (69 distanced [15.0%] and 61 non-distanced [12.8%]; no statistical evidence of a difference: χ 2 (1)=0.78, p=0.376) reported current antidepressant use, with the majority (n=92; 70.8%) taking an SSRI (Table S3).

text.text: For consistency with previous literature, we used the well-characterised model of momentary happiness first described by Rutledge et al. [5] as a baseline model.

This model assumes fluctuations around a baseline (i.e., longer-term mean) can be captured by a weighted sum of recent expected values and prediction errors and, importantly, does not condition on previous ratings.
The Rutledge et al. [5] model has been primarily validated in (e.g., gambling) tasks where expected values and prediction errors are explicitly available to participants 5, 50 .
text.formatted: The Rutledge et al. [5] model has been primarily validated in (e.g., gambling) tasks where expected values and prediction errors are explicitly available to participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> .

text.text: As such, we extended it to account for learning in this task.

Specifically, our model-which we term a joint RL-affect modelcomprised two components: (1) a Q-learning model to infer expected values and prediction errors from participants' choices (which has been shown to accurately capture choice behaviour in this task 40, 41 ); and (2) a model for momentary affect which assumes fluctuations around a baseline can be captured by a recency-weighted sum of Q-learning model-derived expected values and prediction errors 5, 51 .

text.text: Hierarchical models were simultaneously fitted to task choices plus happiness, confidence, and engagement self-reports, assuming different parameter weights across all scales and participants.

A Q-learning model infers expected values (termed Q-values) from participant choices-the action (a t ) of choosing one symbol over the other in each of the three pairs (denoted as states, s t )-by assuming they update at each trial t based on prediction errors δ t , with the update magnitude controlled by a learning rate α ∈ [0, 1]: Q t+1 (s t , a t ) = Q t (s t , a t ) + αδ t , δ t = r t -Q t (s t , a t ).

Here, γ is the discount or "forgetting" factor which imposes a strict weighting on recent trials, and w p k the weights on each of the k quantities of interest for the pth rating type; and Q t ′ and r t ′ are the Q-learning model-derived expected values for the chosen symbol a t ′ in the state s t ′ (i.e., the pair of symbols presented on trial t ′ ) and the feedback valence (±1 for correct/incorrect to allow for negative Q-values) respectively, both at trial t ′ .

Note that both sums are over all previous trials, not just those of rating type p, and all individual-level parameters (w p k , γ p and ϕ p ) were estimated hierarchically (we omit participant indices here for readability).

text.text: All models were fitted to choices and ratings on all three affect scales simultaneously across both distancing and non-distancing participants, with separate weights and decay factors assumed for each person and question, and separate group-level (hyper)priors on each parameter.
In other words, participant-level parameter distributions are assumed to be conditionally independent given the group-level distribution over that parameter.

Individual-level predictive accuracy was assessed by comparing responses predicted from each participant's approximate posterior to their observed affect ratings via pseudo-R² , defined following previous work 52 as the squared correlation between observed and mean posterior predictions.

Drift over time in affect may be particularly relevant to our task, as participants were able to take as long as they wished to rate their subjective feelings, and time between blocks was additionally unconstrained.
As such, we compared the baseline model to four models with different measures of time elapsed (i.e., variants of Equation 5), each with either single or dual learning rates.

text.text: For consistency with computational modelling, we adopt a fully Bayesian approach for statistical analyses where possible.

As such, results are given as estimates with a highest density interval (HDI), which (unlike a confidence interval (CI) 61 ) can be interpreted as the probability that the true value falls within a given range.
text.formatted: As such, results are given as estimates with a highest density interval (HDI), which (unlike a confidence interval (CI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> ) can be interpreted as the probability that the true value falls within a given range.

text.text: We report 95% HDIs to align with convention but interpret results in terms of strength of evidence throughout; an overlap with the null value should not be seen as evidence for lack of an effect, but rather weakened evidence for it.

Alongside HDIs, we report the P direction , which is the proportion of the posterior distribution falling above or below the null value, and has a direct interpretation: the probability the true value falls above or below this null.

We tested the effect of differences in transdiagnostic mental health symptoms, current self-reported antidepressant use, or cognitive distancing on model parameters using generalised linear models (GLMs), adjusted for age, gender, and working memory capacity (measured with visual digit span), separately for each rating type.
GLMs relating model parameters to antidepressant use were run with and without adjustment for concurrent anxiety/depression symptoms (i.e., factor score), as medication use was not randomised.

We also considered whether the effect of cognitive distancing and current antidepressant use on affect model parameters may differ in relation to their association with transdiagnostic mental health, by including factor score as an interaction term in GLMs.

Posterior samples for GLM coefficients were obtained via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented in CmdStan v2.39.0 56 , with 2,000 warm-up and 10,000 sampling iterations for each of four chains, using models and priors from the rstanarm R package 62 .
text.formatted: Posterior samples for GLM coefficients were obtained via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented in CmdStan v2.39.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56</ref> , with 2,000 warm-up and 10,000 sampling iterations for each of four chains, using models and priors from the rstanarm R package <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> .

text.text: Response distributions were assumed Normal for all parameters except for learning and decay rates, which were modelled via Gamma family GLMs (with log link functions).
To aid interpretation, we report estimated betweengroup differences in baseline affect directly on the 0-to-100-point scale.

For differences in the driftover-time, expected value and prediction error weights, we report the multiplicative difference in the odds of the mean affect rating (with 95% HDI and posterior probability of direction), together with an illustrative point-scale translation evaluated for a reference individual with mean baseline affect and median or reference values for the remaining covariates (see Interpretation of GLM-estimated weight effects in the Supplementary Methods for further details).

To account for potential collinearities in the three transdiagnostic mental health symptom factor scores obtained via computational factor modelling, we used partial least squares (PLS) regression to test which of the transdiagnostic factor scores was most strongly associated with baseline affect (w p 0 ).

PLS regression is a data-driven method which identifies latent components linking multivariate responses to predictors based on shared covariance, and so is well-suited to the problem of multicollinearity 63.
text.formatted: PLS regression is a data-driven method which identifies latent components linking multivariate responses to predictors based on shared covariance, and so is well-suited to the problem of multicollinearity <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref>.

text.text: In line with best practice 48 , we first identified the number of components that best described our data in a training set (80% of participants) in terms of mean squared error (MSE) and R² via ten-fold cross-validation.
text.formatted: In line with best practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , we first identified the number of components that best described our data in a training set (80% of participants) in terms of mean squared error (MSE) and R² via ten-fold cross-validation.

text.text: We then validated the predictive accuracy of this number of components in heldout test data (20% of participants), and formally tested this using a permutation test, where the PLS regression model was re-trained on 10,000 training datasets with shuffled outcome labels (providing a null distribution), and the fraction of these datasets where the MSE between the test data and the predictions from the permuted datasets was lower than the true train-test MSE was taken as the pvalue.
The PLS regression with the chosen number of components was then refitted in the whole dataset, to obtain component loadings on each of the responses and predictors.
Lastly, we computed bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CIs for each of the loadings, plus the differences in loadings between transdiagnostic factors, from 10,000 bootstrap samples.

Following model comparison, we found that the best-fitting RL-affect model included separate learning rates for rewarding and non-rewarding outcomes and a linear effect of time elapsed since the beginning of the task (Equation 5; Figure 1D); two alternative parameterisations of the choice model, incorporating differential outcome sensitivity or neglect of negative feedback, did not improve estimated out-of-sample predictive accuracy (Table S1).

text.text: Lastly, we explored whether the negative associations between choice-independent affective dynamics and transdiagnostic anxiety/depression symptoms were altered by cognitive distancing or current antidepressant use, by including treatment by symptom interactions in outcome GLMs.

Here, we applied a computational model of momentary happiness which assumes fluctuations in affect ratings depend simply on baseline affect, its drift over time, and recency-decayed expected and received outcomes.

By extending this model to also capture learning, we were able to link objective behaviour to subjective feelings across distinct affective states-happiness, confidence, and engagement ratings-and show that a core component of psychological therapy, cognitive distancing, and antidepressant medication use have different effects on affective dynamics, but converge to alter affective biases associated with symptoms of mental ill-health.
There were distinct effects of both treatments on affective dynamics.

Randomisation to a psychotherapeutic intervention, cognitive distancing, attenuated declines in happiness and, more tentatively, engagement over the course of the task, adding to our previously reported findings that this psychotherapeutic technique alters aspects of reward learning 41 .
text.formatted: Randomisation to a psychotherapeutic intervention, cognitive distancing, attenuated declines in happiness and, more tentatively, engagement over the course of the task, adding to our previously reported findings that this psychotherapeutic technique alters aspects of reward learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

text.text: Self-reported antidepressant use, meanwhile, was associated with higher baseline happiness and confidence after adjustment for current anxiety/depression symptoms (as antidepressant use was not randomised), which is consistent with evidence that antidepressants exert positive affective biases 64 .
text.formatted: Self-reported antidepressant use, meanwhile, was associated with higher baseline happiness and confidence after adjustment for current anxiety/depression symptoms (as antidepressant use was not randomised), which is consistent with evidence that antidepressants exert positive affective biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> .

text.text: Subsequent exploration of changes in affect revealed further mechanistic divergence: current antidepressant use was associated with lower recency biases for happiness and engagement (i.e., forgetting factors closer to one), and cognitive distancing reduced the weighting of expectations and increased recency bias in happiness ratings.
Together, these results suggest that psychiatric treatments act to alter the contribution of objective learning-related quantities to subjective value judgements.

Consistent with extensive evidence 22, 26, 27, 65 , we found negative associations between model-derived baseline affect (across all scales) and transdiagnostic psychiatric symptom measures derived from computational factor modelling 45, 46 .

text.text: This effect, which was strongest for anxiety/depression symptom scores, indicates a consistent, time-invariant negative affective bias which scales with mental ill-health symptom load.

Critically, we found evidence for a convergent treatment by symptom interaction with baseline affect across both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use: negative associations between anxiety/depression symptoms and baseline happiness and confidence were attenuated in participants receiving either treatment.

These results support the cognitive neuropsychological model of antidepressant action, whereby antidepressants are proposed to act acutely to reverse negative or maladaptive affective biases 21, 66 , and suggest that cognitive distancing 43 and other components of psychotherapy may also act clinically to alter affective biases contributing to symptoms of mental ill-health.
text.formatted: These results support the cognitive neuropsychological model of antidepressant action, whereby antidepressants are proposed to act acutely to reverse negative or maladaptive affective biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66</ref> , and suggest that cognitive distancing <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> and other components of psychotherapy may also act clinically to alter affective biases contributing to symptoms of mental ill-health.

text.text: We propose that changes in affective dynamics should be investigated further in longitudinal studies as a computational predictor of subsequent symptom change.
Our methodological approach also extends previous work in two ways.

First, we applied a theory-driven computational model which allows for fluctuations in momentary happiness as a function of the history of expected values and prediction errors resulting from those expectations, which has been primarily validated in tasks where learning is not required 5 .
text.formatted: First, we applied a theory-driven computational model which allows for fluctuations in momentary happiness as a function of the history of expected values and prediction errors resulting from those expectations, which has been primarily validated in tasks where learning is not required <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: We show not only that this model can capture happiness ratings in a task where expected values are never explicitly available and have to be learned from experience, but also that it can accurately capture variation in subjective ratings of confidence and engagement.
Second, we found evidence for drift in happiness over time, replicating recent work which characterised "mood drift over time" 54 and extending this to both confidence and engagement.
text.formatted: Second, we found evidence for drift in happiness over time, replicating recent work which characterised "mood drift over time" <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> and extending this to both confidence and engagement.

text.text: Affective drift has been proposed to reflect the increasing opportunity cost of remaining engaged, with mood serving as an adaptive signal of the value of continuing (exploiting) rather than switching away from the task (exploring) 54 .
text.formatted: Affective drift has been proposed to reflect the increasing opportunity cost of remaining engaged, with mood serving as an adaptive signal of the value of continuing (exploiting) rather than switching away from the task (exploring) <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> .

text.text: This offers a candidate mechanism for our finding that distancing attenuated drift in happiness: both here and in previous work 41 , distancing participants showed higher inverse temperatures (Figure S2B-C in the Supplementary Methods), indicating more exploitative choice.
text.formatted: This offers a candidate mechanism for our finding that distancing attenuated drift in happiness: both here and in previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> , distancing participants showed higher inverse temperatures (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">S2B</ref>-C in the Supplementary Methods), indicating more exploitative choice.

text.text: Although the inverse temperature cannot distinguish random exploration from other sources of choice variability, in this account attenuated drift and less stochastic choice may both reflect a common shift away from exploration.

We emphasise that this account remains speculative, and that our findings diverged from previous work in two respects: first, rather than reduced drift with increased depressive symptoms during risky decision-making 54 , we found moderate-tostrong evidence to the contrary during RL (Figure 2Aii); and second, drift was strongly associated with self-reported fatigue (Figure S5; see Supplementary Results), which has been proposed to be mechanistically distinct from the boredom that may partly underlie mood drift 15 .
text.formatted: We emphasise that this account remains speculative, and that our findings diverged from previous work in two respects: first, rather than reduced drift with increased depressive symptoms during risky decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> , we found moderate-tostrong evidence to the contrary during RL (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2Aii</ref>); and second, drift was strongly associated with self-reported fatigue (Figure <ref type="figure">S5</ref>; see Supplementary Results), which has been proposed to be mechanistically distinct from the boredom that may partly underlie mood drift <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Both divergences may reflect the demands of our task: where mood drift was previously characterised in rest periods and tasks in which reward contingencies did not have to be learned 54 , sustained learning may render affective drift sensitive to fatigue, meaning that associations between affective drift and symptoms of mental ill-health are not task invariant and likely depend on task demands.

text.text: We note some important limitations in our measures.

Transdiagnostic measures of mental health psychopathology were estimated using questionnaire subsets 41, 48 , precluding investigation of associations between parameters and individual diagnostic scales.
text.formatted: Transdiagnostic measures of mental health psychopathology were estimated using questionnaire subsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , precluding investigation of associations between parameters and individual diagnostic scales.

text.text: Antidepressant use was self-reported and non-randomised, and we did not collect information concerning length of treatment, dosage, concurrent psychological therapies, or reason for prescription; we also could not compare across antidepressant classes, as the vast majority of those on antidepressants (70.8%) reported taking an SSRI (Table S3), though we note this is the class in which affective biases have been most extensively characterised 21.
text.formatted: Antidepressant use was self-reported and non-randomised, and we did not collect information concerning length of treatment, dosage, concurrent psychological therapies, or reason for prescription; we also could not compare across antidepressant classes, as the vast majority of those on antidepressants (70.8%) reported taking an SSRI (Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>), though we note this is the class in which affective biases have been most extensively characterised <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref>.

text.text: We were likewise limited in how well we could characterise the distancing intervention: to minimise differences between groups in task procedure, we did not ask participants about how much they engaged with the intervention, and so lack a direct measure of adherence.

We note, however, that self-rated enjoyment and concentration at the end of the task did not differ between groups, and while in-task baseline engagement (i.e., w engaged 0 ) was lower in the distancing group, this is arguably what one would expect of a technique premised on "taking a step back" from feedback; that this occurred without any corresponding reduction in self-reported concentration suggests emotional rather than attentional disengagement.

Further, cognitive distancing, especially as delivered here, should be considered a treatment component rather than a complete intervention: our parallel analyses with antidepressant use aim to identify points of mechanistic convergence and divergence as opposed to directly comparing the treatments.
We also note two methodological limitations.

First, our use of a single computational model for all three affect scales is a powerful approach, but limited in its ability to truly contrast trial-to-trial fluctuations in each individual rating scale, as we are only comparing the contribution of a small number of computational components (i.e., affective weights) to a fraction of their variation; the residual (scale-specific) variation is likely also important in explaining how these ratings overlap and differ.

This is particularly relevant where the constructs themselves remain contested: momentary confidence may reflect more than the probability a choice is correct 11, 12 , and momentary engagement may index the cost of effort itself or the accumulating cost of continuing 14, 15 .
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant where the constructs themselves remain contested: momentary confidence may reflect more than the probability a choice is correct <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , and momentary engagement may index the cost of effort itself or the accumulating cost of continuing <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Our approach is deliberately agnostic between accounts, asking what can be read out from the trial-wise quantities known to drive choice rather than explaining what each rating specifically measures.

The affect model could in principle be extended with additional weights to distinguish between these accounts, though this would only be informative in a task designed to dissociate quantities such as decision evidence 431 or effort costs from expected values and prediction errors, which ours was not.

Second, as model 432 complexity meant only approximate (mean-field variational, rather than sampling-based) inference 433 was viable, we were unable to account for uncertainty in estimates of individual-level posterior 434 mean parameters in associations with quantities of interest (e.g., by using precision-weighted GLMs), 435 as the posterior covariance matrix cannot accurately capture local interdependencies, meaning that 436 parameter precisions are not reliable enough for uncertainty-weighted outcome models 55,67 .

437 To conclude, we integrated objective choice behaviour in a learning task with trial-to-trial affect 438 ratings across three distinct states-happiness, confidence, and engagement-within a unified com-439 putational model.
This enabled us to uncover associations between model parameters and treatments 440 for mental health conditions, offering new insights into their underlying mechanisms of action.

Our 441 results demonstrate the critical importance of affective biases in the maintenance and updating of 442 affective states in mental ill-health, and indicate that existing, effective treatments can be understood 443 at least in part as acting to shift these biases towards the healthy range.

As such, the lagged trial weight parameters w p 2 (-t ′ ) and w p 3 (-t ′ ) can be seen as capturing the betweenrating change in affective dynamics.

In the Results, effects of covariates on baseline affect (w p 0 ) have a relatively simple interpretation because the second-level GLMs for w p 0 are fitted to the participant-level intercepts after an inverse logit transformation: their coefficients (multiplied by 100) are simply differences in rating points between individuals differing only in the covariate of interest.

Effects on the drift-over-time, expected value and prediction error weights (w p 1 , w p 2 , w p 3 ), meanwhile, are estimated on the log-odds scale, since these GLMs are fitted to the untransformed Beta regression weights.

This means that, for example, a GLM coefficient for the distancing group of 0.1 in relation to w happy 1 for the primary time elapsed model (Equation 5) indicates that the hourly multiplicative change in the odds of mean happiness is exp(0.1) = 1.105 times greater in distanced than non-distanced participants.
text.formatted: This means that, for example, a GLM coefficient for the distancing group of 0.1 in relation to w happy 1 for the primary time elapsed model (Equation <ref type="formula">5</ref>) indicates that the hourly multiplicative change in the odds of mean happiness is exp(0.1) = 1.105 times greater in distanced than non-distanced participants.

text.text: Similarly, multiplicative differences in w p 2 or w p 3 indicate a difference between groups in the multiplicative change in the odds of mean affect for a unit change in (decayed) expected values or prediction errors.

Clearly, these effects do not have obvious interpretations and cannot be directly transformed to the rating point scale, as a fixed difference in log-odds corresponds to a varying difference on the point scale depending on where on the scale it is applied.

To aid in this, we calculate an estimated difference between reference individuals differing only in the covariate of interest (e.g., distanced versus non-distanced; one SD higher symptom score), with the same (mean for that rating type) baseline affect, and all other covariates held at their sample median or reference category.

As this referenceindividual estimate is intended as an interpretive aid rather than a formal posterior summary, we report it as a point estimate alongside the multiplier, its 95% HDI, and P direction.
Our primary model comparison considered two choice model parameterisations: Q-learning models with either one or two learning rates.
This was primarily to maintain consistency with previous work, including the original models of choice behaviour in this task 40 , and our previous work in this sample 41.

text.text: However, differences in choice behaviour, and hence the extent to which choice-related quantities P R E P R I N T are reflected in affect ratings, might be better explained by alternative parameterisations.

In particular, differences in choice behaviours related to anhedonia and depression may be better explained by (in)sensitivity to rewards (outcome sensitivity) than (in)sensitivity to prediction errors (learning rates) 59 .

text.text: To test this proposal, we fitted a variant of our winning RL-affect model with a single learning rate and different sensitivities to rewards ("Correct!") and losses ("Incorrect.").

Another explanation for choice biases stemming from alternative responses to feedback was proposed by Collins et al.

Specifically, they introduce a "perseveration" parameter ζ which allows for potential neglect of negative feedback by reducing the rate of learning from negative prediction errors (α loss ) relative to the rate of learning from positive prediction errors (α reward ): We fitted joint RL-affect models incorporating both alternative choice model parameterisations in an identical manner to our primary model comparison, and then compared their fit to our primary (winning) model with dual learning rates.
Based on the ELPD-LOO, we found no evidence to suggest that either of these alternative models had better estimated out-of-sample predictive accuracy than our winning model (Table S1).

Across individuals, model-predicted baseline affect (w p 0 ) was highest for engagement (mean = 63.4 points; SD = 19.3), followed by happiness (mean = 55.8, SD = 17.3), and lowest for confidence (mean = 40.7, SD = 20.

Meanwhile, affect drift over time (w p 1 ) was steepest for engagement: individual-level median 45.2% lower odds of increased engagement per hour (all other terms being equal), compared to 38.3% lower confidence and 30.0% lower happiness per hour.

Group-level means for weights on recent expected values (w p 2 ) and prediction errors (w p 3 ) were positive for all three ratings, showing higher affect with increased recent rewards, and were lowest for engagement (posterior mean [95% HDI] for multiplier: w happy2 = 1.177 [1.175, 1.179], w confident2 = 1.227 [1.225, 1.230], w engaged2 = 1.129 [1.128, 1.131]; w happy3 = 1.175 [1.174, 1.176], w confident3 = 1.219 [1.218, 1.221], w engaged3 = 1.119 [1.118, 1.120]).

Lastly, the group-level mean decay factor was highest for confidence (mean = 0.543; 95% HDI = [0.541, 0.544]), and lowest for happiness (mean = 0.385; 95% HDI = [0.384, 0.386]), suggesting higher weighting of outcomes of earlier trials (i.e., prior to the most recent trial) in confidence judgements compared to happiness ratings.
Compulsive behaviour and social withdrawal factor scores are also associated with altered affective dynamics

In addition to differences in baseline affect and its drift over time, there was evidence that participants with higher transdiagnostic measures of mental ill-health differed in shorter-term affective dynamics.

Specifically, individuals with higher anxiety/depression factor scores placed more weight on recent prediction errors (higher w p 3 ), with strong evidence for higher w confident 3 (multiplier [95% HDI] = 1.01 [1.001, 1.023] for an SD increase in anxiety/depression score, P direction = 0.986).

There was also strong evidence that those with higher compulsive behaviour scores placed more weight on recent prediction errors, and, to a lesser extent, recent expected values (higher w p 2 ; moderate evidence for higher w happy 2 only) in all of their subjective affect judgements (Figure S3Bii-iii).

text.text: Previous work on 'mood drift over time' has suggested it is mostly distinct from boredom and mind wandering 54 .
text.formatted: Previous work on 'mood drift over time' has suggested it is mostly distinct from boredom and mind wandering <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> .

text.text: Here, we were able to test an additional aspect of this phenomenon, namely its relation to fatigue, as we asked participants the following question after the end of each of the six blocks: "How fatigued do you feel compared to the beginning of the block?".
We hence examined the association between w p 1 and both participants' overall mean post-block fatigue and their change in post-block fatigue ratings over the course of the six training blocks.

To quantify change in post-block fatigue, the six ratings were regressed on block number for each participant, with the regression coefficient (β ∆fatigue ) on block number taken as the quantity of interest (i.e., higher values suggest increases in post-block fatigue ratings over time).

We found strong evidence, after adjusting for age, gender, digit span, and distancing group, that higher mean post-block fatigue ratings were associated with lower baseline affect (lower w p 0 ; Figure S5Ai) and decreased odds of higher affect ratings across the task (lower w p 1 ; Figure S5Aii), across all three affect rating types (e.g.,

To test this, we added an interaction term to the models described above, to test the between-group difference in associations between baseline affect and affective drift, and mean and change in post-block fatigue ratings.

We found strong evidence for an interaction between distancing and fatigue ratings in the as- Figure S5Aiii & Figure S5Biii), such that there were weaker associations between baseline happiness and confidence and fatigue ratings in distancing participants.
text.formatted: We found strong evidence for an interaction between distancing and fatigue ratings in the as- Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S5Aiii</ref> & Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S5Biii</ref>), such that there were weaker associations between baseline happiness and confidence and fatigue ratings in distancing participants.

text.text: In other words, fatigue was less reflected in baseline affect ratings in the distanced group, compared to non-distanced participants.

Crucially, however, we found no evidence of a difference in association between drift in happiness or engagement and either fatigue measure between groups, with weak evidence for differences in the effect of fatigue on confidence (Figure S5Aiv & Figure S5Biv).

text.text: This suggests that the effect of distancing on affective drift is not explained by self-reported post-block fatigue.
We additionally considered whether cognitive distancing may alter associations between Q-learning model parameters and post-block fatigue self-reports.

In distancing participants, each SD increase in anxiety/depression score was associated with 2.10-point higher baseline happiness (95% HDI = [-0.027, 4.21], P direction = 0.974) and 2.04point higher baseline confidence (95% HDI = [-0.409, 4.61], P direction = 0.943) than non-distancing participants (Figure 3Ci).

A similar pattern was seen in those taking antidepressants, though the evidence was clearest for confidence: relative to participants not taking antidepressants with the same symptom levels, each SD increase in anxiety/depression score was associated with 5.07-point higher baseline confidence with strong evidence (95% HDI = [0.809, 9.26], P direction = 0.991), and, with (very) weak evidence, 1.44-point higher baseline happiness (95% HDI = [-2.10, 4.95], P direction = 0.785; Figure 3Cii).
